parsed_answer.content:
The Spring Framework is an inversion-of-control (IoC) container and a comprehensive programming model designed to simplify enterprise Java development. At its core, Spring solves the 'plumbing' problem of Java EE by decoupling application components through Dependency Injection (DI). Instead of objects manually instantiating their dependencies—which creates tight coupling and makes unit testing nearly impossible—the Spring IoC container manages the lifecycle, configuration, and assembly of these objects, known as Beans. By abstracting away low-level boilerplate code, Spring allows developers to focus on business logic while providing a consistent, modular architecture that scales from microservices to monolithic enterprise systems.

Beyond simple dependency management, Spring provides a massive ecosystem of modules. Aspect-Oriented Programming (AOP) allows developers to modularize cross-cutting concerns like logging, security, and transaction management, injecting them into business methods without polluting the source code. The framework also integrates seamlessly with data access layers (Spring Data), web services (Spring MVC), and security protocols (Spring Security), effectively acting as the 'glue' that holds modern Java applications together. It transforms the JVM from a mere execution environment into a robust, high-performance platform for distributed computing.

items: The IoC Container manages the Bean lifecycle, moving through stages: instantiation, population of properties, BeanPostProcessor initialization, and destruction callbacks.
Spring AOP uses dynamic proxies (JDK proxies for interfaces, CGLIB for classes) to intercept method calls, enabling declarative transaction management via @Transactional.
The ApplicationContext is the central interface for providing configuration information to the application, typically implemented via XML, annotations, or Java-based configuration classes.
Spring's design relies heavily on the 'Inversion of Control' principle, shifting the responsibility of object creation from the application code to the framework infrastructure.

parsed_answer.content: A common production pitfall is the 'Circular Dependency' error. If Bean A requires Bean B, and Bean B requires Bean A, the IoC container cannot finish the instantiation process. While Spring can resolve some circular dependencies via setter injection, it is a major architectural smell indicating that your components are too tightly coupled; always prefer constructor injection to enforce immutability and fail-fast initialization.
